title: Can someone share their AI game they've made?
author: EliasWick
selftext:
I keep reading how great AI is all the time in this thread and I would actually like to see what people are creating. My stance and trust that AI is able to produce something fantastic without a lot of human intervention is very low. Please prove me wrong, I welcome it!

Share your Steam pages, and screenshots and what not. I'm not to judge you or the work, I just want to know how good it is and be proven wrong.

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
Well, prompting could be considered human intervention. But what I mean is playtesting, actually writing your own code, creating your own animation, audio, music etc.

Of course AI can do all that, but it's unlikely to come together well at this time.

replies.author: CubersumGame
replies.body:
Once again, you haven't defined the boundaries.

My game was created using AI - the code, the music, the localization came from AI.

But I worked on it for over eight months. Without that work, there would be no game at all.

That is why I am asking: what does "intervention" mean, and where are its limits?

Otherwise, it’s just a way to dance around the issue - saying, "Well, this game might be good because there was human intervention, but actually, AI is bad."

Define the parameters first - then ask your questions.

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
Sorry, I didn't explain myself very clearly. I can see how my text can come across as dismissing for the eight months you spent making your game.

When I say human intervention, I mean making deliberate decisions that shape how the game actually plays and feels. Things like tweaking mechanics, balancing difficulty, changing the pacing, testing what works, and scrapping things that don't. You can do all of that while using AI. You don't need to write every line of code yourself for your contribution to matter. Although not to make things more confusing, I believe code to be an artform itself. So, if you don't write the code yourself, the project is in my eyes "less" expressive. Same as for the music and everything else. I understand that people don't have money, time or experience; and you should be able to tell your story or create things as well. Just for me personally, I think the project itself is losing out on a lot of quality through the use of AI. Again, I still see the usefulness in it and I understand that new developers find it super great for progress.

The line I'd draw is between accepting whatever AI produces because it runs, and working with it to make something that meets your own goals. Can you spot what's wrong? Do you have an idea of what would make it better? Are you making changes and checking whether they actually help? That's the kind of involvement I'm talking about. I can't give you a meaningful minimum number of hours or percentage of handwritten code, because neither would tell us much about those decisions.

Based on what you've described, your eight months of work sounds like it fits that definition. The fact that AI produced the code, music, and localisation doesn't erase everything you did to turn those parts into a finished game.

People could make games before AI, and using AI still takes effort. My point was that it's becoming easier to produce something that technically qualifies as a game. Getting it to run is one thing. Making it enjoyable, polished, and worth someone's time is another.

I'd put more weight on how well the game plays than on the fact that someone managed to build it. And that should apply whether they used AI or made everything themselves. As a tech artist I value proper performance optimisation, and that's rarely something you get from AI.

Plenty of great games build on familiar ideas and concepts. That's basically how we do things today, originality is very rare... Being different just for the sake of it doesn't make a game good either. A better question would be: what does your game do well, and what makes someone want to keep playing it?

I still think human judgement plays a big part in making a good game. But you're right that I can't just say "AI is bad" and then credit human involvement whenever an AI-assisted game turns out well. That would make my argument impossible to challenge.

If your game is good, it's good. Using AI shouldn't disqualify it, just as spending eight months on it doesn't automatically prove its quality. The finished experience is what we should judge. My point is that the decisions you made during those eight months matter, even if AI did a lot of the production work.

And, to cap off, if you take a look at the games here from others, it's mostly web based ones which is a little telling of AI. It's awesome that people are creating things, and the things people have posted here looks really solid. Although, before AI we had very limited number of browser games.

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
Again, if you are afraid that I would decompile your game, it's unlikely that I would have an interest in playing it. Many games shared here are really good, and I know that there is a current situation where people are threatened to get their games stolen, which sucks.

My opinion still remains true for ME; if I can decompile your game or re-create it with AI easily, it's not something I have an interest in re-creating or likely play. For instance, try re-creating Minecraft. You'll very quickly run into issues. It's a seemingly "simple" looking game, but under the hood it's not.

If your game took a week to make, then it's going to take someone a similar time to re-create it, or even faster. If the game takes 5 years with a team of 100 people, it's extremely difficult for you to even replicate a small portion of it.

If you have a look at the games here, most are browser or Godot based. If I had a proprietary engine with custom tech, it's even better for me.

Honestly Kytheon, I understand why you hide your post and comment history. You have all the right to be scared and uncomfortable regarding people stealing other peoples work. But if we stretch things, AI should be unethical in some sense in your eyes too then, right? How much work and data should I need to train my model before it's "fine" to use other peoples contents?

comments.author: LowenbrauDel
comments.body:
I made a digital adaptation of the JAWS board game. Reddit keeps auto deleting my post about it (probably due to the external links to google drive or something). Here's a [youtube link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lFn6OkKSl0o) for the trailer for this, in the description you'll find links for the gameplay footage

Obviously, not made to be released due to the IP. But it was a passion project about favorite franchise and the curiosity of 'can AI actually do that or will it fall apart?'. Which I guess is the same question you have

I wouldn't say that this project was 'AI game' in common sense of the word. There was a lot of handmade stuff in it. But Claude basically did all the coding. I had to explain the rules, how they would work in the game, design the bots, how they would think, how the UI would look like, the assets. Like, it was not a type of 'hey, here's this game, make it digital' and AI just one-shotted the whole thing from scratch. But if you put your mind to it, AI is the great tool to help you out in areas which you're not qualified

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
That's pretty neat! I used to play the pinball version at the office quite a bit. I am not sure how much similar the board game is to that, but I'm glad to see it.

You could perhaps re-brand it? I know a colleague who designed his own board game and is now turning it into an actual game in Godot. I am curious how much troubles you've had with balancing and modifying the code? I myself do both art and code from scratch, but I know artists typically want to avoid fiddling with code if they can.

replies.author: LowenbrauDel
replies.body:
Friends jokingly told me the same thing about re-branding, like call it "FANGS" or something =)) However, I am honest about it not really being fully mine, gameplay mechanics wise, so I don't want to fool anyone. I am currently developing something of my own, and that's what really opening your eyes to the whole 'game development' process. AI really does open the doors, but you soon realize that only you alone can determine whether the game is actually fun or not. And now I truly understand how actually hard it is to make an original and interesting game. Like, before AI I only thought that coding was the true hard part. Nope. The hard part is idea itself. That, of course, if you really care about the game being fun and all =)

I didn't change a single line in code myself. And Claude, surprisingly understood really well what I wanted from him. Wasn't always like that, I've noticed that he was starting to lose track of the bigger picture. In the end, however, I managed to get our plan synchronized and the get the results I wanted from him. Sometimes it took one iteration, sometimes five. Then again, it was my first big project in Claude. Like, I barely knew about .md files, context, instructions and all that. Right now, with my own project, I planned the whole thing from the start, created several chats for its own task, make chats more to the point and wrap them up as soon as the session goal is completed

Tl;dr version is this: if you make a plan and stick to it, you can keep everything on rails. As for the code my layman position is if the game does what I want it to do, then the code works and I don't need to see what's inside of it. Then again, I am not dealing with complex backend situations and I don't have to maintain the game code. I made it, it works, I play the game, why would I change the code?

comments.author: GazMagal
comments.body:
Hey! I've been working on **Six Zero League**, a browser-based 2D handball management game.

The game is currently in alpha, with 242 registered accounts so far. Development is very much driven by player feedback. I regularly get feedback from people who enjoy handball as well as players who are into sports management games, and that feedback is shaping the game as I build it.

The idea is to combine the depth of a sports management game with an incremental/progression loop. You manage your club, develop your players, make tactical decisions and watch your team play matches through a live 2D simulation.There's still a lot to improve and plenty of features I want to add, but the core experience is playable now.

If you're interested in handball, sports management games, or just trying something a little different, I'd love for you to give it a try.

🔗 [**https://sixzeroleague.com**](https://sixzeroleague.com)

I'm particularly interested in hearing what you think about the progression, management mechanics and match simulation. Even critical feedback is welcome, that's a big part of how I'm developing the game. Currently there's just one type of competition (league), with 2 matches every day at 12:00 PM and 8:00 PM (Europe/Lisbon).

Thanks for checking it out!

https://reddit.com/link/pggv87u/video/y888yzyr98vh1/player
